chapter: Swing, singers, Ed Fox and recordings
title: Budd Johnson and the Hines arrangers
summary: Budd replaced Cecil; Irwin, Mundy and Budd did most arranging.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: We were talking about Earl discovering talent today. And you said he found Trummy Young and Billy Eckstine in Washington. Where did Budd Johnson come from? I know he was from Texas, and then he was in Kansas City for a while, or --
Right off hand I can't remember. Budd was around here. Where did we pick up Budd?
He came about 1935, I think. Well, I guess after Cecil --
After Cecil. See, because Cecil and Mundy was the two tenor players, and then when Cecil got killed, then we got Budd Johnson.
Budd's an awfully talented man.
Yes, he is.
His arrangements and --
Very good arranger.

-- playing. Very good player. Seems like a lot of the guys, as they came in the band, started contributing to the library. When Mundy was in the band was he -- did he do most of the arranging? Or Cecil Irwin when he was in the band?
When Cecil Irwin was in the band, he did most of the arranging. Then when Mundy come in, it was between him and Cecil. And I had a few little tidbits in between.
Well, after Cecil was killed and Mundy left, did Budd start doing most of the arrangements?
Yeah. Yeah.
At that time, the mid-thirties, was it still this arrangement of the publisher, you know, pay the arranger?
Yeah. In the mid-thirties, yeah.
About how many new arrangements would you have in say a month's time, with the band?
Oh, sometimes we'd have five or six new arrangements a week.
Really? For the show or --
No, the band. You know, just pop tunes.
Truck Parham told me that bands -- there would be real competition among the arrangers, to see who could --
Yeah, you'd try to outdo one another.
Yeah.
